sentences.text: The genus Parahelicoprion contains two species: one from Russia and another from Bolivia.
Both species share tooth crowns featuring long, backwards-sweeping recessed lower sections and curved denticles along their edges.
The holotype of the Russian species measures 25 cm in profile and includes six articulated tooth crowns plus a smaller fragment.
Teeth increase significantly in size toward the rear of the whorl, while those farthest forward are rounder and more asymmetrical than the nearly symmetrical rear teeth.
The rear edges of the frontmost tooth crowns form sharp, non-serrated cutting blades.
The genus Parahelicoprion was formally described by Karpinsky in 1924.
Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi was described by Merino-Rodo and Janvier in 1986.
The holotype of the Russian species consists of tooth fragments that were damaged by mining and broken into pieces.
The holotype of the Bolivian species consists of nine partial teeth with broken outer edges.
The type specimen of the Russian species was found in the Ural Mountains of Russia in Artinskian strata.
Karpinsky considered it likely that parts of the holotype were destroyed by mining or never collected.
Due to incomplete fossils, estimates of size and ecology are speculative, though it is assumed to have been large, predatory, and potentially pelagic.
Parahelicoprion was a carnivore that lived in marine environments.
The type species of the genus is Helicoprion clerci.
Xystracanthus grandis and Physonemus mirabilis have been suggested as potential synonyms for Parahelicoprion.
Parahelicoprion belongs to the family Helicoprionidae within the order Eugeneodontiformes.
The family Helicoprionidae is defined by possessing tooth whorls with forward-angled, blade-like tooth crowns and often completely fused tooth roots.
Parahelicoprion lived during the Early Permian.
Parahelicoprion fossils from the Copacabana Formation date to the boundary between the Carboniferous and Permian periods.
Researchers suggest that the layer preserving the fossils in the Copacabana Formation formed in a shallow, intertidal habitat.
Authors have suggested the Bolivian species had a short tooth whorl at the tip of elongated jaws, but acknowledged the material is too fragmentary for confident comparison.
Researchers debate whether large fin spines found with the genus correspond to edestoids, copulatory organs of symmoriiform fishes, or holocephalans.
It is debated whether crushing teeth similar to Campodus or Orodus were present, as no other teeth are confidently associated with the species.
